entries.modern_form: Bailey's Iranian base *gan- 'to seize' (abstracted from Khotanese uysgana- 'vulture' < *uz-gana- 'seizing out, rapacious'), which Bailey attaches to PIE *gʰend- / *gʰed- 'to seize, grasp' (Pokorny IEW 437 f.)
entries.note: The root box is a faithful copy of H. W. Bailey. In his Dictionary of Khotan Saka, s.v. uysgana-, Bailey writes verbatim: 'From uz-gana- "rapax" of a bird of prey, N.Pers. zaγan … Hence a base gan- "to seize", IE ghen- to IE Pok. 437-8 ghen-d-', and again in the reverse index 'gan- "to seize", in the name of the raptor bird uysgana- "vulture"'. So the base, the gloss and the whole chart are Bailey's, and Nourai reproduces them accurately. Two reservations keep this from 'confirmed'. (1) 'Indo-Schythian' is not a language: it is the title of Bailey's series (Indo-Scythian Studies = Khotanese Texts), and the language of uysgana- is Khotanese Saka, an Eastern Middle Iranian language of the Tarim basin, 5th-10th c. CE. (2) *gan- 'to seize' is Bailey's own back-formation from a single compound; it is not an independently attested Iranian verb, and the PIE root he links it to (*gʰend-, Pokorny 437 f., AHD ghend-) has no Iranian reflex in Pokorny, Walde-Pokorny or Watkins — its witnesses are Greek χανδάνω, Latin prehendere/praeda, Germanic *getan (English get, beget, forget) and Celtic. Nourai does not repeat Bailey's IE link, which is prudent.
entries.note_fa: جعبهٔ ریشه در این نمودار عیناً از هارولد بیلی گرفته شده است. بیلی در «فرهنگ ختنی-سکایی»، ذیل uysgana-، می‌نویسد که این واژه از *uz-gana- «رباینده» است و «از این‌جا ستاکی gan- به معنی گرفتن/ربودن به دست می‌آید» و آن را با ریشهٔ هندواروپایی *gʰend- (پوکورنی ۴۳۷ به بعد) می‌سنجد؛ پس نقل نورایی درست است. اما دو نکته: نخست آنکه «هندوسکایی» نام هیچ زبانی نیست، بلکه عنوان مجموعهٔ کتاب‌های بیلی است و زبان این واژه ختنی-سکایی (ایرانی میانهٔ شرقی) است؛ دوم آنکه ستاک *gan- ساختِ خودِ بیلی از یک ترکیب است و در هیچ متن ایرانی به‌تنهایی گواهی نشده، و ریشهٔ هندواروپایی‌ای که بیلی به آن پیوند می‌زند در پوکورنی و والده-پوکورنی و واتکینز هیچ بازماندهٔ ایرانی ندارد. بنابراین ادعای نورایی «با احتیاط پذیرفتنی» است.

nodes.derivation: The form is exact: Bailey (DKS s.v.) cites 'Z 13:35 uysgani' — the Book of Zambasta, the great Khotanese Buddhist poem of the 5th-6th c. CE — as the manuscript spelling (altered from an older uysguni), rendering Buddhist Sanskrit gṛdhra- 'vulture', and quotes JS 24v1 'pura pemesti aysgani … the vulture seized the young ones in its sharp beak' and K 21:4 aysgana-rrūvyi 'in vulture-form'. Morphologically uysgana- = uz- 'out, away' (Av. uz-, OP ud-) + gana- (verbal adjective of the base gan- 'to seize'), i.e. 'the one that seizes/snatches away', Latin rapax; Khotanese writes the prefix uys- because Old Iranian *uz- before a voiced stop gives uys- (the same uys- as in uysāna- 'to raise'). The vulture is therefore named exactly as Sanskrit gṛdhra- is named from gardh- 'to seize', as Latin voltur is from vellō 'to pluck, seize', and as Yidgha yereno (in kyāl-yereno 'bald eagle') is from *gṛdnu- — the parallels Bailey himself lists. The only caveat is the language label: this is Khotanese Saka, not a language called 'Indo-Scythian'.

nodes.derivation: This node reproduces the last, deliberately tentative sentence of Bailey's article: 'Possibly Sogd. VJ γn'w "force".' VJ = the Sogdian Vessantara Jātaka (Paris, Pelliot sogdien 4, 8th-9th c.), and Bailey's suggestion is that a Sogdian abstract γn'w 'force, might' could contain the same base gan- 'to seize' (semantically 'grip' > 'strength'). The link is unconfirmed by Sogdian lexicography: B. Gharib's Sogdian Dictionary (1995) — the standard word-list, and Nourai's own second reference here — has no entry γnw or γan on p.163 or anywhere in its γn- run, and the gloss 'skill' that Nourai adds appears in neither Bailey nor Gharib (Gharib's word for 'skill' is qnw'ncya, no. 4784, unrelated). So the word may exist as a hapax reading in VJ, but the node as drawn — a Sogdian noun 'power, force, skill' descending from the base gan- — is a possibility flagged by Bailey rather than an established derivation.

nodes.derivation: New Persian زغن zaγan 'kite, Milvus, a black bird of prey' is a real and old word: Asadi Tusi's Loghat-e Fors (11th c.) glosses غلیواج as 'مرغ گوشت‌ربای، به معنی زغن بود', and Borhan-e Qate' has 'زغن و خاد (هم) مرغ گوشت‌ربای بود' with the Rudaki couplet Nourai quotes. Bailey derives it, exactly as the chart does, from the same Old Iranian *uz-gana- 'seizer' that gives Khotanese uysgana-: initial *uz- loses its vowel in the West Iranian development (*uzgana- > *zagan-, cf. NP زدن/زن- beside Av. jan-), and intervocalic -g- is kept as -γ- and written غ. The chart's arrow, however, makes زغن descend from the Khotanese word, which it does not: Bailey lists NP zaγan as a parallel outcome of *uz-gana- in another Iranian branch, i.e. a cognate, not a borrowing from Khotanese — Khotanese was never a donor to Persian. Nourai's own second reference is the right place to look: Mo'in's footnote to the زغن entry in Borhan cites Bailey's BSOS X and Transactions of the Philological Society 1946, p.159 n.1. Modern lexicography adds nothing against it (Wiktionary has no Persian entry at زغن at all, only an Arabic verb), so 'plausible' rather than 'confirmed'.
nodes.derivation_fa: «زغن» به معنی پرندهٔ شکاریِ گوشت‌ربا (غلیواج) واژه‌ای کهن است: اسدی طوسی در «لغت فرس» غلیواج را «مرغ گوشت‌ربای، به معنی زغن» می‌داند و برهان قاطع بیت رودکی «جمله صید این جهانیم ای پسر / ما چو صعوه، مرگ برسان زغن» را برای آن می‌آورد. بیلی آن را از همان ایرانی باستانِ *uz-gana- «رباینده» می‌گیرد که در ختنی uysgana- «کرکس» شده است؛ در شاخهٔ غربی واکهٔ پیشوندِ *uz- افتاده و ‑g‑ میان‌واکه‌ای به غ نرم شده است. اما پیکانِ نمودار نادرست است: «زغن» از واژهٔ ختنی گرفته نشده، بلکه هم‌ریشهٔ آن است؛ ختنی هرگز زبانِ وام‌دهنده به فارسی نبوده است. حاشیهٔ معین بر برهان قاطع نیز همین‌جا به مقالات بیلی ارجاع می‌دهد. بنابراین ریشه‌شناسی پذیرفتنی است ولی رابطهٔ دو گره باید «هم‌ریشگی» خوانده شود نه «اشتقاق».

entries.modern_form: PIE *gang- 'to mock, jeer' (Pokorny IEW 352; Walde-Pokorny I 535), an onomatopoeic root, beside the parallel sound-words *gong-/*guñg- 'to mutter, hum'
entries.note: Pokorny's page 352 opens with exactly this headword: 'gang- "spotten, höhnen"; gango-s "Hohn"', with Skt. gañja-ḥ 'contempt, mockery', Gk. γαγγαίνειν (Hesychius) 'to mock', OE canc, ge-canc 'scorn, derision' (= Skt. gañja-ḥ), cancettan 'to mock', ON kangen-yrði 'mocking words'. Nourai's gloss 'to mock, hum' is a compression of two things Pokorny keeps a little apart: 'mock' is the root proper, and 'hum' comes from Pokorny's closing remark that 'Die Sippe scheint ursprüngl. schallmalend. Ähnliche Schallwörter sind ai. gúñjati "summt, brummt", gr. γογγρύζειν "grunzen" … aksl. gągnavъ "schwer sprechend", russ. gugnati "murmeln"'. Since these are the words the chart's own Sanskrit and Persian nodes hang on, the compression matters and is discussed at node 1. Root, language label and Pokorny page number are all correct.

nodes.derivation: Sanskrit guñj (present guñjati) 'to buzz, hum, murmur' is real and well attested (of bees, of a muttering voice), and it is an imitative formation. The question is the arrow. Pokorny does not derive guñjati from *gang-: he closes the *gang- article with 'Die Sippe scheint ursprüngl. schallmalend. Ähnliche Schallwörter sind ai. gúñjati "summt, brummt", gr. γογγρύζειν "grunzen", spätgr. γογγύζω "murre", aksl. gągnavъ "schwer sprechend", russ. gugnati "murmeln", poln. gęgać "schnattern"' — i.e. guñjati is listed as a similar but independent onomatopoeia beside *gang-, with -u- vocalism against the root's -a-. Walde-Pokorny (at gou-, WLD I) is more generous and says outright that guñjati belongs 'unter *gang- "spotten"'; Mann sets up a separate root gong- 'mutter, murmur' for the same word. Since expressive roots do not obey regular ablaut, all three positions are defensible; Nourai has simply adopted the most generous one. Note also that Pokorny's Sanskrit witness for *gang- proper is gañja-ḥ 'contempt, mockery', not guñj-.

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian gung 'dumb, mute' is solidly attested: MacKenzie, Concise Pahlavi Dictionary, prints 'gung [g(w)ng | N ~] dumb', and Nyberg's glossary 'gung [gwng, gng] dumb 11°. 127. 652°', citing the Pahlavi Rivāyat and the Shāyast nē Shāyast passage 'bē kē karr ayāb gung ēnyā …' ('with the exception of the deaf and the dumb'). What cannot stand as drawn is the arrow from Sanskrit: Middle Persian does not descend from Sanskrit, and no loan is involved either — there is no route by which an Indo-Aryan present stem guñj- could become a Sasanian Persian adjective. What the sources give is a comparison, and a nervous one: Horn, Grundriss no. 937 (p.209) writes 'gung "stumm". skr. √guñj-, guñjati "summen, brummen" (Geiger: "das Brummen bezeichnet die tierischen Laute des Stummen im Gegensatz zur menschlichen Sprache"). Unsicher.' and Hübschmann's note on the same number (Pers. Stud. p.95) is a bare 'Höchst unsicher.' Wiktionary phrases it the same way: MP gung, 'perhaps developed from the sense "to mock, hum", usually connected to Sanskrit guñjati … itself of imitative origin'. Read as 'cognate with / compared with', the node is fine; read as descent, it is not.

nodes.derivation: New Persian گنگ gong (classical gung, Tajik гунг, Dari gung) 'mute' continues Middle Persian gung directly and without change: the MP short u is preserved in the classical and eastern pronunciation and lowered to o only in modern Iranian Persian (gung > gong), the same way MP gurg > Ir. Pers. gorg. Wiktionary states 'Inherited from Middle Persian gwng /gung/, gng /gung/ "dumb, mute"'; Farrokhi's line, which Nourai prints and which Mo'in also prints in the footnote to Borhan 1844, 'گنگ باد آنکس که اندر طعن تو گوید سخن / کور باد آنکس که اندر عرض تو جوید عوار', shows the word already in the 11th century with exactly this sense. One inaccuracy of gloss: گنگ means 'mute, unable to speak', not 'deaf' — Persian for deaf is کر (MP karr), and the Pahlavi and Borhan passages set karr and gung side by side as two different disabilities. 'Deaf' in the chart is an artefact of the English idiom 'deaf and dumb'.

entries.modern_form: Young Avestan gaṇtuma- / gantuma- m. 'wheat' (Bartholomae, AiW col. 493), Proto-Iranian *gantuma-, whence NPers. gandom
entries.note: Bartholomae's Altiranisches Wörterbuch gives the headword verbatim: 'j. gantuma- m. "Weizen"', with the Nirangistan passage 'unter den Getreidearten ist es der Weizen, der den Frawašis genehm ist' (N 28); Wiktionary lists Avestan gaṇtuma / gantuma among the cognates of گندم. The root box's language label and gloss are therefore right. The chart's added note, 'Cognate with Sanskrit gōdhūma', is also right and is precisely what Nourai's two references say: Hübschmann, Persische Studien p.95 ad Horn 935, 'Skr. gōdhūma- wird volksetymologische Anlehnung von *gandhūma- an die Composita mit gō- "Kuh" sein (go-dhūma- gleichsam "Kuhrauch"; vgl. unsern Pflanzennamen Erdrauch)', and Buck 516 §8.48.7, 'Skt. godhūma-, by pop. etym. (cpd. of go- "cow" and dhūma- "smoke") for *gandhuma- = Av. gantuma-, NPers gandum "wheat", root connection? Barth. 493.' Both mark the pre-Indo-Iranian source as unknown — 'root connection?' — so the word is best treated as an inherited Indo-Iranian agricultural term of ultimately obscure (very possibly non-IE, Central Asian) origin, which is why Nourai wisely heads the chart with an Avestan and not a PIE box.

nodes.derivation: The Middle Persian word is certain, though the spelling in the chart is the Pazand one. In Book Pahlavi the word is written with the Aramaic heterogram ḤNṬH (Aramaic ḥinṭā 'wheat'), so MacKenzie's dictionary prints 'gandum [Hz < A ḥnṭh | (M gnwm), N ~] wheat', with the Manichaean Middle Persian spelling gnwm as the phonetic control; Wiktionary likewise cites Manichaean 𐫃𐫗𐫇𐫖 (gnwm) and Parthian gndwm. The form 'gantum' with -t- is what the Pazand transcriptions of the Pahlavi glossaries give, and it is Horn's own citation, no. 935 p.209: 'phlv.-paz. gantum d. i. gandum (PPGl.)' — Pazand spelling gantum, real value gandum. Phonologically Av. gaṇtuma- > MP gandum by the regular voicing of a stop after a nasal in Middle Persian (*-nt- > -nd-, as in Av. bandaka- > MP bandag) and by the reduction of the thematic ending. So the node is right, with the caveat that gantum is a graphic, not a phonetic, Middle Persian form.
nodes.derivation_fa: واژهٔ فارسی میانه قطعی است، اگرچه صورتی که در نمودار آمده صورتِ پازند است. در پهلویِ کتابی این واژه با هزوارشِ آرامیِ ḤNṬH نوشته می‌شد؛ از این رو مکنزی می‌نویسد «gandum [هزوارش < آرامیِ ḥnṭh | (مانوی gnwm)، فارسی نو ~] گندم» و صورتِ مانویِ gnwm را گواهِ تلفظ می‌گیرد؛ ویکی‌واژه نیز صورتِ مانویِ gnwm و پارتیِ gndwm را می‌آورد. صورتِ gantum با «ت» همان است که در آوانویسیِ پازندِ واژه‌نامه‌های پهلوی آمده و خودِ هرن (بند ۹۳۵، ص ۲۰۹) می‌نویسد: «پهلوی-پازند gantum یعنی gandum». از نظر آوایی، اوستاییِ gaṇtuma- در فارسی میانه به gandum بدل شده است، زیرا در فارسی میانه همخوانِ بی‌واکِ پس از خیشومی واکدار می‌شود (nt < nd، مانندِ bandaka- > bandag) و پایانهٔ ستاکی می‌افتد. پس گره درست است، با این توضیح که gantum صورتی نوشتاری است نه تلفظی.

nodes.derivation: All three are correct. (1) گندم gandom continues MP gandum unbroken (classical gandum, still gandum in Dari and Tajik, gandom only in modern Iranian Persian); the variants the chart puts in brackets are ordinary Persian derivatives — گندمک gandomak, the diminutive in -ak (also a name of the smallpox-like rash), and گندمینه gandomina, the adjectival -ina 'of wheat'. Wiktionary's chain is the chart's: NPers گندم < MP gnwm/gandum < Proto-Iranian, beside Parthian gndwm, Sogdian γntm, Kurdish genim, Pashto غنم, Avestan gaṇtuma-, Sanskrit गोधूम. (2) گندمگون gandomgun 'wheat-coloured, olive-complexioned' is گندم + گون, the Persian colour suffix from MP gōn 'colour, kind' (Av. gaona- 'hair, colour'), whence Nourai's cross-reference to his chart Gěu; the Hafez line the JSON records, 'خال مشکین که بدان عارض گندمگون است', is the classic occurrence. (3) گندم‌با gandom-bā (dialectal گندم‌وا) 'wheat pottage' is the dish now called حلیم/هلیم; -با is the old Persian word for a cooked broth or stew (as in زیرباج/سکباج), which Nourai refers to his chart Pekw, i.e. to PIE *pekʷ- 'to cook' — a link that is plausible but not demonstrable from Middle Persian, and Mo'in's own footnote is content to analyse the compound as 'گندم + با (=آش)'. The Persian forms in the JSON match the printed page exactly.
nodes.derivation_fa: هر سه واژه درست است. ۱) «گندم» دنبالهٔ بی‌گسستِ gandum فارسی میانه است (در دری و تاجیکی هنوز gandum، و gandom تنها در فارسیِ ایران)؛ صورت‌های داخلِ کمانک ساخته‌های عادیِ فارسی‌اند: «گندمک» با پسوندِ تصغیرِ ‑ک و «گندمینه» با پسوندِ نسبتِ ‑ینه. زنجیرهٔ ویکی‌واژه همان زنجیرهٔ نمودار است: فارسیِ گندم ← فارسی میانهٔ gnwm ← ایرانی آغازین، در کنارِ پارتیِ gndwm، سغدیِ γntm، کردیِ genim، پشتوِ غنم، اوستاییِ gaṇtuma- و سنسکریتِ गोधूम. ۲) «گندمگون» از گندم + گون است؛ «گون» از gōn فارسی میانه (اوستایی gaona- «مو، رنگ») که نورایی آن را به نمودارِ Gěu ارجاع می‌دهد؛ بیتِ حافظ «خال مشکین که بدان عارض گندمگون است» شاهدِ کلاسیکِ آن است. ۳) «گندم‌با» (گویشی: گندم‌وا) همان خوراکی است که امروز حلیم می‌گویند؛ جزءِ «با» واژهٔ کهنِ فارسی برای آش و خورش است (مانندِ زیرباج و سکباج) و نورایی آن را به ریشهٔ *pekʷ- «پختن» می‌برد، که پذیرفتنی است ولی از فارسی میانه اثبات‌پذیر نیست؛ حاشیهٔ معین خود به تجزیهٔ «گندم + با (=آش)» بسنده می‌کند. صورت‌های فارسیِ ثبت‌شده در داده‌ها با چاپِ کتاب دقیقاً می‌خواند.

entries.note: Bartholomae's Altiranisches Wörterbuch has the headword in this exact shape: 'j. garənav- m. "Krätze"', with the Vidēvdād passage the entry quotes; Horn no. 895 (p.200) locates the attestations, 'aw. garənu- "Krätze" vd. 7,58 (145), yt. 13,131'. Nourai's language label and gloss are therefore right, though 'Krätze' is scabies/mange in man and beast alike, so 'scab on animal skin' is narrower than the Avestan word. One genuine dispute the chart does not show: the meaning of the Avestan word has been read three ways. Darmesteter and Jackson took it as 'Krätze'; Geldner (KZ 25, 551) translated 'Sonnenglut' (the blazing of the sun); Bartholomae himself, in the earlier Arische Forschungen/Studien II 96, read 'Frost' and compared Latin gelū, OCS žlědica, German kalt. Horn accordingly ends 'also unsicher'. Bartholomae's mature Wörterbuch of 1904 abandoned his own earlier reading and printed 'Krätze', which is the view Nourai's chart, Mo'in's footnote in Borhan and modern Iranian lexicography follow.

nodes.derivation: A Middle Persian gar 'scab, mange' is asserted by all the older Iranists but is missing from the standard modern concise lexica. Horn no. 895 (p.200) ends his entry 'phlv. gar', and Mo'in's footnote in Borhan p.1779 sources it precisely: 'پهلوی gar (جرب) «دارمستتر، تعلیقات ج۱ ص ۹۵»', i.e. Darmesteter's notes to his Zend-Avesta, where the Pahlavi Vidēvdād renders Av. garənu- by gar. Formally the derivation is unproblematic: an Old Iranian u-stem *garnu- / garənav- loses its suffix in Middle Persian and appears as a bare gar, with the doubled -rr of the New Persian word (garr) reflecting the assimilated cluster. But MacKenzie's Concise Pahlavi Dictionary has only 'gar [gl] mountain' and no gar 'scab' (its list runs gar - -gar - garān - garasmān - gard …, and its English-Pahlavi part has no 'scab', 'mange' or 'itch' at all), and Nyberg's glossary likewise has only 'gar [gl] mountain … Av. (513 sq.) gari-'. So the etymon is well motivated and supported by the Pahlavi Vidēvdād glosses, but not attested in the dictionaries a modern reader would check first — hence 'plausible' rather than 'confirmed'.

nodes.derivation: The etymology of both words is sound; the flag is on the Persian script of the second one in the JSON. (a) گَرّ garr 'mange, scabies (which makes the hair fall out)' continues MP gar < Av. garənav-, and the Arabic equivalent Borhan gives is جرب; Nāser-Khosrow's couplet in the chart, 'گر نخواهی رنج گر از گرگنان پرهیز کن / جهل گر است ای پسر پرهیز کن زین زشت گر', plays on the word and on the homophone گر 'if'. The bracketed variant گَری garī is the abstract in -ī, 'scabbiness'. (b) گَرگِن gargen / گَرگین gargin 'scabby, mangy; bald' is گر plus the Persian adjectival suffix -gīn (MP -gēn, as in خشمگین, شرمگین, نمگین), with the by-form -gen; Mo'in's footnote to Borhan p.1779 states exactly this pairing, 'مریض را «گرگین» (مخفف آن: گرگن) گویند', and Nāser-Khosrow's plural گرگنان in the very verse the chart prints shows the short form was the living one for him.
